findings.location: Problem Formulation; Methodology; Appendix B; reading table row 1
findings.feedback: The note accurately separates fixed DAG decomposition and generated metadata from planner decisions. The planner produces agent assignment and cross-edge retention rules; an interpreter expands a compact script. The simulator follows a fixed topological order and serializes tasks on each agent. These are controlled scheduling assumptions, not measured worker behavior or evidence of an optimal scheduler. The note also preserves the disabled shared-rate-limit waiting limitation.

findings.location: Equations 1–7; Appendix G; reading table row 2
findings.feedback: The account correctly treats geometric parent-quality propagation, retention powers, clipping/lower bounds, terminal macro averaging, and equal-weight quality/time/token score as constructed simulator functions. The robust/balanced/fragile exponents 0.35/0.85/1.25, 2.5% pre-compression package token charge plus one time unit, and 1200 startup tokens plus two time units match the text. Nothing here establishes real semantic fidelity, provider billing or elapsed-time prediction, and the note correctly rejects a Pareto guarantee.

findings.location: Appendices A, F-III, G; Tables 10 and 20; reading ablation row
findings.feedback: The note correctly highlights the important modeling choice: an omitted cross-agent transfer multiplies its upstream quality contribution by lambda=0.5 but adds no communication tokens, time or stored context. Removing the penalty, normal auto-completion, and auto-completion plus lossless compression are different ablations, with normal completion charging resource costs. Shrinking score separation establishes sensitivity to the chosen mechanisms; it does not calibrate their realism. Applying this permissive fallback to the repository required-evidence gate would be unjustified; the note explicitly refuses that transfer.

findings.location: Tables 1–3; Appendix D-I; reading validation row
findings.feedback: The correlations are over six model-level averages, not task-level predictions or independent per-run samples. The reported two-sided exact-permutation p-values and key values match: final score Pearson r=.816, p=.047; Spearman rho=.771, p=.103; removing Doubao leaves Pearson r=.421, p=.500. The latter is an important small-sample sensitivity, retained by the note. Positive leave-one-model-out coefficients alone do not establish stable predictive accuracy.

Actual handoffs are inferred using output keywords in later prompts, and simulated versus real ILR use different definitions and denominators. Table 2 time/token Pearson values are negative (-.264/-.607) and non-significant (.633/.206); positive quality correlations across four frameworks do not repair resource-prediction validity or imply a causal effect. The note preserves these distinctions and the need for target-framework validation.

findings.location: Tables 4–9; Appendix G; reading experiment row
findings.feedback: The main 240-DAG study, four nominal sizes, shared fixed 50-problem cap/context sweeps and ten fixed problems per extreme size are represented faithfully. Transfer-coverage/quality correlations are partly induced by the scoring function and should not be read as independent causal evidence. Five high-disagreement tasks versus random selection support a limited screening example, not global non-degradation or a universal routing policy; the note says so.

The note attributes the 3.754 to 4.150 out-of-five mean real score increase to the authors’ 20-task study, with DeepSeek-V4-Flash execution and DeepSeek-V4-Pro evaluation, rather than this repository or an independently established success rate. Each candidate adds one simulation-selected cross-role handoff, or keeps B=A if none improves simulation. The simulated speed and token-efficiency declines are retained, so quality improvement is not presented as free.

findings.location: Appendix F-II; Tables 6 and 19; reading counterexamples paragraph
findings.feedback: The note retains the distributional counterexample: at 128k, multi-agent simulated quality is lower in 82% of model–problem pairs even though the overall mean advantage is +.007. The positive mean is driven by the 100-task group; smaller nominal groups already favor the single agent. This is a simulator/context-pressure result, not a universal statement about real MAS quality.

findings.location: Appendix E-III; Table 14; reading DAG-validation row
findings.feedback: The 24/70=34.3% quantity is rejection by at least one successful LLM judge, not an independently certified semantic error rate. The 82 error mentions overlap across DAGs. Table 14 normalizes each category as p_fail*c_m/82 to partition the failure mass; its row percentages are not separate category incidence rates. The note preserves this unusual denominator and avoids summing overlapping rates as independent outcomes.

The note correctly rejects reading Table 16 scores as pass rates or averaging the visible columns into Overall. Deterministic scores use capped issues/N with structural penalties included in Overall; LLM dimensions are 0–100 judgments with holistic Overall. Large-DAG judges receive metadata, summaries and sampled rows rather than full JSON, so their scores cannot certify all hidden semantic dependencies. The 500-node DAG-assistance experiment is only ten real tasks, accuracy 2/10 to 3/10 and mean 3.300 to 3.575; no broad efficacy claim is justified.

findings.location: Appendix G and Algorithms 1–2; reading inference/cost row
findings.feedback: One deterministic simulation does not mean one total LLM call. Each model–problem pair has one primary planning call and, on parse/validation failure, one repair call; DAG generation separately has seed filtering, generation/refinement and judges. A total-cost claim must account for the relevant roles and amortization. The reading expressly retains these costs instead of equating simulated tokens with all-role provider usage.

findings.location: Table 8; Appendix C; reading counterexamples paragraph
findings.feedback: The claimed 74x token and 9.7x time reductions compare simulation-based evaluation with real execution, not deployed worker savings. Table 11 has historical-best Top-3 comparisons that are competitive or better; Table 12 keeps MAE at .088 despite adding complexity features. The note includes these qualifications rather than reporting only favorable headline results.

findings.location: DAG Construction; Appendix E-II; Appendix G
findings.feedback: k99 is derived using deterministic list scheduling and a threshold C+.01(W-C). Its 99% refers to the attainable reduction relative to W-C under this construction, not 99% absolute runtime accuracy or a proof of optimal scheduling. Context windows are assigned from generated/estimated working sets and mapped to 16/32/64/128k; the note correctly does not treat these as measurements of full provider input loading.

findings.location: reading final paragraph; frozen TASK, Plan62 prefix and recovery report
findings.feedback: Repository applicability is appropriately limited to adapting an evaluation distinction: dependency existence versus actual information delivery, followed by validation on the real target host. No new simulator, pool, automatic edge completion, compression-power policy or model ranking is authorized or claimed. Existing single TASK, MemoryLedger, directed handoffs and consumer-controlled required references remain the stated basis. Strategy adoption is deferred until trusted backend evidence, same-state real-task comparisons, complete corrections/dissent/dependencies, all-role usage/cost and independent acceptance are available.

optional_findings.feedback: For maximum precision, qualify the short phrase Overall含额外结构罚 as rule-based Overall, and add that LLM Overall is holistic. The existing note already correctly says scores are not pass rates and not the mean of visible columns, so this is a non-blocking clarification rather than a required correction. The distinction is fully preserved in F10 of this original review.

The phrase 34.3%失败质量 could be clearer as 34.3%失败概率质量 or 失败样本占比的归一化分解, to distinguish probability mass from the simulator quality variable Q. The immediately adjacent explanation and 24/70 denominator make the intended meaning recoverable; no scientific claim depends on the wording.
